amendment.text: Chicago has its own toilet-count table and rules (Section 18-29-403 and Table 18-29-403.1 of the Chicago Plumbing Code, rewritten by the 2021 amendments), different from the Illinois Plumbing Code's Table B. The table applies to new buildings, additions and changes of occupancy. Occupants are the building code's occupant load, split half male and half female; fractions round up. Restaurants and bars: men 1 per 30 up to 90 then 1 per 50, women 1 per 25 up to 100 then 1 per 30. Offices, schools through 12th grade and factories: one figure, not split by sex (1 for the first 10, 2 for 11 to 25, 1 more for each 25 above 25). Urinals are optional: they may replace up to 67% of required water closets in separate facilities in assembly and educational occupancies and up to 50% in other occupancies (20% in all-gender rooms). One single-user toilet room is enough for a building or tenant space with 30 or fewer occupants. No public toilets are required for stores under 7,500 sq ft, quick-transaction spaces with a public area of 400 sq ft or less, or parking garages. Each toilet used by the public or employees needs its own compartment with a door (at least 30 in wide and 60 in deep for a floor-mounted toilet, 56 in for wall-hung); each urinal needs partitions at least 30 in apart, starting no more than 12 in above the floor and reaching at least 60 in.
amendment.quote: 18-29-403.1 Minimum number of fixtures. For new buildings, additions and changes of occupancy, plumbing fixtures shall be provided in the minimum number shown in Table 18-29-403.1, based on the intended use of the building or space. [...] Table 18-29-403.1 [Water closets, Male | Female] Assembly: Restaurants, banquet halls and food courts; nightclubs, bars, taverns, dance halls and facilities for similar purposes: 1 per each 30 to 90; 1 per each 50 above 90 | 1 per each 25 up to 100; 1 per each 30 above 100. Business: Facilities for the transaction of business, professional services, other services involving merchandise, banks, ambulatory care, light industrial activities and similar uses [one cell across Male and Female, shared with Educational and Factory and industrial]: 1 for first 10; 2 for 11 - 25; 1 additional for each 25 in excess of 25. Educational: Education of children through the 12th grade level and child day care not classified as an institutional occupancy. [...] a. One fixture is required for the number of persons indicated or any fraction of the number of persons indicated. | 18-29-403.1.1 Number of occupants. The total number of occupants shall be the occupant load determined in accordance with Section 1004 of the Chicago Building Code provided that such number may be reduced based on nonsimultaneous occupancy or access controls. Where separate facilities for each sex are required by Section 18-29-403.2 or the number of occupants of each sex is required by Table 18-29-403.1, the number of male occupants and the number of female occupants shall be the total number of occupants divided in half. | 18-29-403.1.2 Minimum fixture calculations. To determine the required number of fixtures, the fixture ratio or ratios for each fixture type shall be applied to the number of occupants or the number of occupants of each sex in accordance with Table 18-29-403.1. Fractional numbers resulting from applying the fixture ratios of Table 18-29-403.1 shall be rounded up to the next whole number. [...] Exception: One single-user toilet room in accordance with Section 18-29-403.1.3 shall be acceptable for a building or tenant space with an occupant load of 30 or fewer. | 18-29-419.2 Substitution for water closets. In each bathroom or toilet facility, urinals shall not be substituted for more than 67 percent of the required water closets in separate facilities in assembly and educational occupancies. Urinals shall not be substituted for more than 50 percent of the required water closets in separate facilities in all other occupancies. Urinals shall not be substituted for more than 20 percent of the required water closets in nonseparate facilities. | 18-29-405.3.4 Water closet compartment. Each water closet utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate compartment with walls or partitions and a door enclosing the fixtures to ensure privacy. | 18-29-405.3.5 Urinal partitions. Each urinal utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate area with walls or partitions to provide privacy. The horizontal dimension between walls or partitions at each urinal shall be not less than 30 inches (762 mm). The walls or partitions shall begin at a height not greater than 12 inches (305 mm) from and extend not less than 60 inches (1524 mm) above the finished floor surface.

worked_examples.how: Business row, one figure for both sexes (1 for first 10; 2 for 11-25; 1 additional for each 25 in excess of 25), applied here to each half of the occupants: 25 per sex gives 2 each. Applied to all 50 at once it gives 3 for the building. Urinals may replace up to 50% of the men's 2: 1.

Business row, one figure for both sexes (1 for first 10; 2 for 11-25; 1 additional for each 25 in excess of 25), applied here to each half of the occupants: 50 per sex gives 2 + 25/25 = 3 each. Applied to all 100 at once: 2 + 75/25 = 5 for the building. Urinals: up to 50% of 3, so 1.

Business row, one figure for both sexes (1 for first 10; 2 for 11-25; 1 additional for each 25 in excess of 25), applied here to each half of the occupants: 100 per sex gives 2 + 75/25 = 5 each. Applied to all 200: 2 + 175/25 = 9 for the building. Urinals: up to 50% of 5, so 2.

Business row, one figure for both sexes (1 for first 10; 2 for 11-25; 1 additional for each 25 in excess of 25), applied here to each half of the occupants: 200 per sex gives 2 + 175/25 = 9 each. Applied to all 400: 2 + 375/25 = 17 for the building. Urinals: up to 50% of 9, so 4.

Restaurant row: men 1 per each 30 to 90 and 1 per each 50 above 90; women 1 per each 25 up to 100 and 1 per each 30 above 100. 25 per sex: men 25/30 = 0.83, so 1; women 25/25 = 1. Urinals: up to 67% of 1 is less than one fixture.

Restaurant row: men 1 per each 30 to 90 and 1 per each 50 above 90; women 1 per each 25 up to 100 and 1 per each 30 above 100. 50 per sex: men 50/30 = 1.67, so 2; women 50/25 = 2. Urinals: up to 67% of 2, so 1.

Restaurant row: men 1 per each 30 to 90 and 1 per each 50 above 90; women 1 per each 25 up to 100 and 1 per each 30 above 100. 100 per sex: men 90/30 = 3 plus 10/50 = 0.2, total 3.2, so 4; women 100/25 = 4. Urinals: up to 67% of 4 = 2.68, so 2.

Restaurant row: men 1 per each 30 to 90 and 1 per each 50 above 90; women 1 per each 25 up to 100 and 1 per each 30 above 100. 200 per sex: men 3 plus 110/50 = 2.2, total 5.2, so 6; women 100/25 = 4 plus 100/30 = 3.33, total 7.33, so 8. Urinals: up to 67% of 6 = 4.02, so 4.
Educational row (same figure as Business), applied to each half: 25 per sex gives 2 each (3 for the building if applied to all 50). Urinals: up to 67% of 2 = 1.34, so 1.
Educational row (same figure as Business), applied to each half: 50 per sex gives 3 each (5 for the building if applied to all 100). Urinals: up to 67% of 3 = 2.01, so 2.
Educational row (same figure as Business), applied to each half: 100 per sex gives 5 each (9 for the building if applied to all 200). Urinals: up to 67% of 5 = 3.35, so 3.
Educational row (same figure as Business), applied to each half: 200 per sex gives 9 each (17 for the building if applied to all 400). Urinals: up to 67% of 9 = 6.03, so 6.

fixtures.reading_note: Offices, schools and factories share one water closet cell that spans the Male and Female columns. Section 18-29-403.1.2 says the ratio applies to 'the number of occupants or the number of occupants of each sex in accordance with Table 18-29-403.1', and Section 18-29-403.1.1 halves the occupants where separate facilities are required. The worked examples apply the figure to each half (W/M cells); applied once to all occupants it gives one toilet fewer for the building at each of the four sizes (3, 5, 9, 17 in total instead of 4, 6, 10, 18). The per-sex reading equals or exceeds the Illinois Plumbing Code office row at every size. Confirm with the Department of Buildings.
fixtures.state_comparison: Against the state pack: Chicago needs more women's toilets in restaurants (2/2 at 100 against the state's 1 and 1 plus urinal) and more in schools than the state's elementary row. For high schools the state's separate row asks 1 women's toilet per 20 (10 at 400 occupants) and urinals for men; Chicago has one school row (9 and 9 at 400, urinals optional). Which applies to a Chicago high school is a question for the Department of Buildings; public schools also fall under the State Board of Education's code (state pack).

restrooms_city.rule: Chicago's plumbing code (2021 amendments) adds detail to the state's Equitable Restrooms Act. Single-user toilet rooms must be identified as available to all persons regardless of sex or gender, have an occupant-controlled lock that shows from outside when the room is occupied, be enclosed by walls or partitions from floor to ceiling, and contain a covered waste receptacle. A shared toilet facility with at least three water closets and two lavatories may serve all genders if each water closet is in its own compartment with solid walls or partitions and a single door, with no gaps between 4.5 inches and 7 feet above the floor when the door is closed and the enclosure (other than the door) reaching at least 9 feet or to within 2 inches of the ceiling; each compartment has an occupant-controlled lock with an occupied indicator and a covered waste receptacle; urinals, if any, are in marked lockable compartments or a visually separated area, with partitions from no more than 12 inches to at least 7 feet above the floor; a single-user toilet room is within 200 feet when the shared room has more than three water closets; and the main entrance door cannot be locked while the area is occupied. Arenas, stadiums and convention halls keep separate facilities in the numbers the state Act requires.
restrooms_city.quote: 18-29-403.1.3.1 Signage. Single-user toilet rooms and single-user bathing rooms shall be identified as being available for use by all persons, regardless of their sex or gender. 18-29-403.1.3.2 Lock. The door to a single-user toilet room or single-user bathing room shall have a locking mechanism controlled by the occupant. When engaged, the locking mechanism shall visually indicate to those outside the room that the room is occupied. [...] 18-29-403.1.3.4 Waste receptacle. Single-user toilet rooms shall contain a covered waste receptacle. | 18-29-403.2.1 Nonseparate facilities. Where a toilet facility containing at least three water closets and two lavatories is intended to serve all persons, regardless of their sex or gender, it shall comply with the requirements of Sections 18-29-403.2.1.1 through 18-29-403.2.1.5. [...] 18-29-403.2.1.2.1 Enclosure. Each compartment shall be enclosed with solid walls or partitions. Each compartment shall have a single door. When the door is closed, there shall be no gaps in the enclosure between 4.5 inches (114 mm) and 7 feet (2134 mm) above the floor. Portions of the enclosure other than the door shall extend to at least 9 feet (2743 mm) above the floor or to 2 inches (51 mm) below the ceiling, whichever is less. Compartments may be fully enclosed. 18-29-403.2.1.2.2 Lock. The door to each compartment shall have a locking mechanism controlled by the occupant. When engaged, the locking mechanism shall visually indicate to those outside the compartment that the compartment is occupied. 18-29-403.2.1.2.3 Waste receptacle. Each compartment shall contain a covered waste receptacle. 18-29-403.2.1.3 Urinals. Urinals, where provided, shall be located in clearly marked individual compartments with lockable doors or in an area of the toilet facility that is visually separated from other portions of the toilet facility. Urinal partitions shall begin at a height not greater than 12 inches (305 mm) from and extend to not less than 7 feet (2134 mm) above the finished floor surface. 18-29-403.2.1.4 Proximity to single-user toilet room. A single-user toilet room shall be provided outside of, within 200 feet (70.0 m) of, and not more than one story above or below the entrance to nonseparate toilet facilities containing more than three water closets.
restrooms_city.summary_quote: Adopt provisions for optional multi-stall all-gender restrooms and require gender-neutral signage for single-user toilet rooms.
restrooms_city.conflict_note: Chicago's 2021 text allows urinals in a shared all-gender room (in lockable compartments or a screened area). The state's later Section 30 of the Equitable Restrooms Act (in force August 11, 2023, 'notwithstanding any other provision of law') says an all-gender multiple-occupancy restroom shall not contain urinals and requires floor-to-ceiling dividers and a privacy strip. Whether Chicago amended its text after 2023 was not checked (current code not readable).

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Chicago job sites. Price your restroom, see Chicago's own toilet counts and the rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Chicago office towers, schools, restaurants and event venues, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** Chicago has its own building rules. They treat toilet partitions as an interior finish and require solid plastic (HDPE) and polypropylene partitions to pass a room-corner fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Chicago has its own plumbing rules, separate from the state's. They set the number of toilets by how many people use the building, and every toilet used by staff or the public needs a stall with a door. The table further down shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Chicago requires a building permit for most construction, alteration and repair work. Its list of work that needs none covers painting, tiling, cabinets, countertops and similar finish work, and movable partitions no taller than 7 feet that aren't fixed in place. It doesn't name fixed toilet partitions, so ask the Chicago Department of Buildings (312-744-3449) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** in Illinois every one-person restroom in a public building or a place open to the public must be marked as a restroom for all genders, with no gender on the sign. Chicago adds a lock that shows from outside when the room is in use and a covered waste bin. A shared restroom may be made all-gender. In Chicago each toilet then sits in its own compartment with solid walls and one door, with no gaps between 4.5 inches and 7 feet above the floor, walls that reach 9 feet or to within 2 inches of the ceiling, a lock that shows when it is in use and a covered waste bin inside. Illinois law also requires dividers from floor to ceiling, a privacy strip at the door and no urinals, and in a newly built or converted room a menstrual supply dispenser and a baby changing station.
page.stalls_intro: Chicago counts toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. Half are counted as men and half as women, and any part of a group counts as a whole one. Every toilet needs a stall with a door. The counts apply to new buildings, additions and changes of use. Urinals are optional. In restaurants and schools they may take the place of up to two thirds of the men's toilets, and in offices up to half. Each urinal needs a screen on both sides, at least 30 inches apart and reaching at least 5 feet above the floor.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums for the whole building. For offices and schools the city's table gives a single figure, not one for men and one for women. The numbers here apply it to each half of the building's capacity. Applied to the whole building at once it gives one toilet fewer, so confirm the count with the Chicago Department of Buildings. A space for 30 people or fewer may have one single-user restroom. Stores under 7,500 square feet and takeout counters with no more than 400 square feet of public area need no public restroom. At least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Chicago's building rules count an office at one person per 100 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. The plumbing rules allow a lower number where not everyone is in the building at the same time. Your architect or the Chicago Department of Buildings sets the final number.
page.install_rule: Chicago licenses general contractors by class, from A to E by project value, through the Department of Buildings, and asks for liability insurance before a contractor can pull permits. The city requires a licensed and insured general contractor for most building work. Illinois has no state license for partition installers. Confirm what your job needs with the Chicago Department of Buildings. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: Chicago requires a city-licensed and insured general contractor for most building work.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on state, county, city and school district projects, and other work paid for with public funds, Illinois law requires at least the wage the Illinois Department of Labor sets for each trade in each county. For a carpenter in Cook County that is $58.51 an hour plus $46.82 in health, pension, vacation and training contributions.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 10.5% in Chicago: 6.25% state, 1.75% Cook County, 1.25% city and 1.25% regional transit. The transit part rose by a quarter point on August 1, 2026.
page.buyers_extra: - **Arenas, convention halls and event venues:** HDPE or phenolic where crowds and nightly washdown are hard on stalls. Illinois law sets its own toilet numbers for these venues.

page.official_names: - The rules by their official names: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design; Illinois Accessibility Code (71 Ill. Adm. Code 400), 2018 edition; 2019 Chicago Building Code (Municipal Code of Chicago Title 14B, based on the 2018 International Building Code), mandatory for permit applications started on or after August 1, 2020, with accessibility in Chapter 14B-11, as amended by the Construction Codes Modernization Phase 3 ordinance (SO2026-0024930), mandatory from December 1, 2026; Chicago Plumbing Code (Municipal Code of Chicago Chapter 18-29, referenced by Title 14P), the 2001 code with the 2021 amendments, mandatory from March 1, 2022; Administrative Provisions of the Chicago Construction Codes (Title 14A), Section 14A-4-402 for work exempt from permits; Equitable Restrooms Act (410 ILCS 35); NFPA 286 for HDPE.
notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether a like-for-like replacement of fixed toilet partitions needs a Chicago building permit (Department of Buildings, 312-744-3449, or the assistance counter on the 9th floor of City Hall).

To confirm with the Department of Buildings: whether the single toilet figure for offices, schools and factories in Table 18-29-403.1 applies to each sex (as in the page's table) or to the whole building (one toilet fewer at each size).

Read the current Municipal Code in a browser before launch (American Legal Publishing blocks automated access; the city's read-only ICC copies show a captcha): Sections 18-29-403, 18-29-405.3 and 18-29-419.2 for amendments after October 2021, Section 14A-4-402 (permit exemptions) and Sections 14B-8-803 and 14B-10-1004 (read on UpCodes only).

Chicago's 2021 text allows urinals in a shared all-gender restroom if they are in lockable compartments or a screened area; the state's 2023 law says such a room has no urinals. The page states the state rule. Ask the Department of Buildings which it applies.

Phase 3 code amendments become mandatory for permit applications started on or after December 1, 2026. The ordinance was searched and does not change toilet counts, interior finishes, floor area per person or toilet room rules, so the page carries no bullet for it. The Commissioner's transition memo (CodeMemo2026-001) could not be opened: read it once.
The city still describes a full rewrite of the Chicago Plumbing Code as under study: recheck the stall table when it is adopted.

For high schools the Illinois Plumbing Code's own row asks more women's toilets (1 per 20) and urinals for men than Chicago's single school row; a local code must be at least as strict as the state's. Ask the Department of Buildings which count it applies to a high school; public schools also follow the State Board of Education's code.

Chicago also taxes non-titled goods bought from a seller outside the city at 1% (Use Tax for Non-Titled Personal Property, Municipal Code 3-27-030, per the city's glossary). Whether it applies on top of the 10.5% to partitions shipped in from out of state was not researched: a question for Abe's accountant.

The Illinois state pack's source bullet for toilet counts cites the Illinois Plumbing Code table and prints in this page's Sources list, although Chicago applies its own table: the state pack text is right for the rest of Illinois, so leave it and rely on the Chicago bullet above it.
Sales tax: the January 1, 2027 rate change summary was not yet on the Department of Revenue's bulletin list; recheck in December.
Cook County prevailing wage rates were reposted on 11/18/2026; the Department of Labor revises them during the year. Which classification covers partition installation was not read.

The Illinois state pack's access bullet says the office that issues the building permit checks the plans; in Chicago the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities also reviews accessibility (per the city's permit help page). Chicago's own accessibility chapter (14B-11) was not compared with the Illinois Accessibility Code.
